sections.h2: Who values and who bills property in Webster County?
sections.html:
In Webster County one office sets the value and another sends the bill. The Assessor sits in Room 19 of the Marshfield courthouse at 417-859-2169, and the Collector sits in Room 15 at 417-859-2683. Mail for the Collector goes to P.O. Box 288, Marshfield, MO 65706.

The Collector's site names Kevin Farr as the officeholder. It says the office brings in about $27 million of tax revenue each year, issues merchant licenses and conducts the delinquent tax sale every August. The counter stays open through lunch on weekdays until half past four.

The Assessor's page describes the task as putting fair market value on property as of the tax date. Two bodies can review that work: the county Board of Equalization and the Missouri State Tax Commission. The page links online personal property filing and a county GIS map. GIS access is a paid subscription arranged by phone.

Rates are a separate matter. Each taxing body adopts its own, and the county's Taxes page shows 2025 rates by school district.

sections.h2: When does a Webster County tax bill come due?
sections.html:
Webster County bills go out in November and are payable as soon as they arrive. December 31 is the cutoff. A check bearing that day's postmark or earlier is on time, while a later one is returned unless the late charges are enclosed.

Webster County Collector rules for the tax year, as posted on the Collector's site
TopicRule
StatementsMailed in November, due upon receipt
DeadlinePostmarked December 31 to avoid penalty and interest
Missing statementContact the office if none arrives by the end of November
Older yearsDelinquent years are paid before current taxes are accepted
Mail paymentsEnclose the bottom portion of the statement
In-person paymentsBring the statement
Delinquent tax saleHeld in August

Anyone paying late follows the schedule printed on the lower part of the statement. Under state law the postmark date is the payment date, and registered or certified mail uses its certification date instead.

sections.h2: How are Webster County homes valued for tax?
sections.html:
Missouri taxes residences on 19 percent of market value. Marshfield's own page repeats that figure along with 32 percent for commercial and industrial property, and says the county does the assessing and collecting for the city.

New real estate values are set in odd-numbered years and stay in place the following year except for new construction. That puts the next general reset on January 1, 2027. A planned increase above 15 percent on a house, improvements aside, calls for a visit to the property. Driving past does not meet the requirement, and the owner has no less than 30 days after the written notice to request an interior look.

  • Houses: 19 percent of true value.
  • Agricultural land: 12 percent.
  • Commercial and industrial: 32 percent.
  • Personal property: 33 and one-third percent, lower for livestock and farm machinery.

sections.h2: How do you contest a Webster County assessment?
sections.html:
Phone the Assessor at 417-859-2169 once a change notice lands, and ask how to set a hearing. The Board of Equalization comes first. Should the Board hold its number, the State Tax Commission is next, with a filing window of 30 days after the Board acts or the chapter's own date if that is later.

Payment need not wait. An owner who settles the entire current bill ahead of delinquency may give the Collector a written protest, and the disputed portion is parked in a separate account. That protest dies unless the owner sues the Collector in circuit court inside 90 days. A person with a timely Commission appeal pending skips the lawsuit, and a winning taxpayer receives the interest the fund earned.

The Assessor's page describes the State Tax Commission as the state agency with general supervision over assessors and the job of enforcing property tax law. The Assessor says it has no say over the budgets of the taxing bodies, so a high rate is a question for the school board, city or fire district rather than the Assessor's counter.

sections.h2: Is a senior tax freeze open in Webster County?
sections.html:
The 2026 application window for the senior citizens' property tax credit ran May 1 to June 30, 2026, so it has closed. Applicants had to be 62 before January 1, 2026, and the credit reaches residential real estate tax on a primary home. It holds the bill at 2026 base year levels. It is a freeze, and it does not exempt anything.

Two kinds of tax stay outside it: levies the state constitution guarantees, such as the blind fund and general obligation bonds, and voter-approved increases adopted after the base year. Vehicle tax and other personal property tax are excluded too. Forms were taken at the County Clerk's office in Room 12, with photo identification, a utility bill or voter card as proof of residency, and last year's paid receipt. The Clerk's line is 417-859-8683. Ask the Clerk when the next window opens, and what a mid-year sale does to an approved freeze.

sections.h2: What does the Marshfield city levy add to a bill?
sections.html:
Marshfield property owners pay the city's levy on top of the school, county and special district rates. After voters approve general obligation bonds, the Board of Aldermen sets a debt service rate high enough to cover principal and interest. The parks and cemetery levy has a ceiling that only voters can lift. That ceiling lets collections rise by 5 percent or the Consumer Price Index, whichever is lower, against the prior year.

The county Taxes page breaks its 2025 rate tables into Diggins, Fordland, Marshfield, Niangua, Rogersville, Seymour and Strafford school districts, plus rural Webster County. Match the district printed on your statement, not the mailing city.

sections.h2: How do you pay a Webster County bill?
sections.html:
• At the Collector's counter, with the statement in hand.
  • By mail, with the bottom portion of the statement enclosed.
  • On the Collector's website by e-check, debit or credit card, where cards add a convenience fee.
  • Accepted forms: cash, personal check, money order, cashier's check. One check can pay several bills.

The Collector says it is not responsible if you pay tax on property that belongs to someone else or skip a parcel you own, so check the account number against your parcel. A statement that never reached you does not erase the tax, penalty or interest.

sections.h2: What do Census figures say about Webster County households?
sections.html:
Webster County counted 36,202 people in the 2010 census and 39,085 in 2020. The 2020 to 2024 survey counts 13,964 households and finds 87.6 percent of residents in the same house a year before. The county is home to 2,990 veterans.

Owners occupy 77.4 percent of occupied homes, the lowest share of Stone, Warren and Webster, so renters have a larger presence here. Landlords get their statements in November like other owners and face the same December 31 postmark date.

The county is part of the Springfield metropolitan area. Six cities (Fordland, Marshfield, Niangua, Rogersville, Seymour and Strafford) and the village of Diggins make up its municipalities. Marshfield, at 1,490 feet, is the state's highest county seat, and its courthouse of Carthage marble dates from 1939 to 1941.

faqs.q: When do Webster County property taxes become delinquent?
faqs.a: After December 31. Each statement is payable on arrival, and mail needs a postmark dated on or before the 31st.

faqs.q: Where is the Webster County Collector located?
faqs.a: Room 15 of the courthouse, 101 S. Crittenden Street, Marshfield. Mail goes to P.O. Box 288, and the phone is 417-859-2683.

faqs.q: Can I pay a Webster County bill by card?
faqs.a: Yes. The Collector's site takes cards, e-checks and debit, and card payments add a convenience fee.

faqs.q: Is the Webster County senior freeze accepting applications?
faqs.a: Not now. The 2026 window ended June 30, 2026. The County Clerk at 417-859-8683 can say when the next opens.

faqs.q: Who decides Webster County tax rates?
faqs.a: Each taxing body does, meaning schools, cities, fire districts and the county. The Assessor and Collector do not.
